findings.title: Arena/zone depth for a call site is computed with 0 as "unset", so a later deeper `mut ref` argument raises it: caller passes a too-short-lived arena -> heap-use-after-free
findings.why: `argDepth[k] == 0` means "this destination lives outside the caller's frame" (a parameter or a global) and is the SHALLOWEST, longest-lived destination; the comment on the following line says exactly that ("an argument at depth 0 already forces the home arena"). But `0` is also the sentinel for "no minimum seen yet", and `if (nd == 0 || d < nd) nd = d;` lets any later positive depth overwrite it. The result is a maximum, not a minimum: with argDepth = {0, 1} the loop yields nd = 1, so `want = (nd <= 0) ? ARENA_HOME : nd` passes `&__extc_a[1]` (a block of the caller's frame, destroyed on return) instead of `__extc_home`. The callee's home-arena allocation is therefore placed in an arena that dies before the destination that receives it -> the reference the callee stored through the out-parameter dangles. The identical bug is duplicated in the zone counterpart at lines 6326-6334 (`for (int k = 0; k < rec->n; k++) { ... if (nd == 0 || d < nd) nd = d; }` + `zwant = (nd <= 0) ? ZONE_HOME : nd`), where a pool would be born in a place that dies before its owner. The correct shape is the one used by hand for `h` at lines 1290-1317 (`haveDest || d2 < h`), i.e. an explicit "first element" flag; the following line `if (nd == 0 && rec->n > 0) nd = rec->n ? rec->argDepth[0] : 0;` is a no-op after the loop and cannot repair it.
findings.trigger: A callee whose effect summary records at least two `mut ref` argument positions (e.g. the standard out-parameter shape `fn stash(dest: mut ref slot, other: mut ref slot, v: i64) { @overwrite var n = new node  n.value = v  dest.v = n }`), called with argument 0 pointing outside the caller's frame (a parameter or a global) and a later argument pointing at a local declared in a deeper block, e.g. `fn caller(dest: mut ref slot) { var deep: slot = { v: null }  stash(dest, ref deep, i64(5)) }`. The fresh value the callee stores into `dest` is placed in `&__extc_a[1]` of `caller`, which `extc_arena_destroy` frees when `caller` returns, while `dest` (owned by `caller`'s caller) still points at it. Any program reading that slot afterwards is a use-after-free; the compiler reports no diagnostic.

findings.title: `countOwSites` does not descend into `ST_DOMAIN`, while codegen's `collectOwSites` does: an `@overwrite` inside `d.run { }` makes the compiler emit a cell of a type it never declares
findings.why: The header comment of this function claims "The order must match codegen's `collectOwSites`: both walk the same tree in source order, so the n-th site here is the n-th cell there." That invariant is not established: codegen's walker has `case ST_DOMAIN: collectOwCallsExpr(s->u.domain_.callee, out); collectOwSites(s->u.domain_.body, out); return;` (src/codegen.c:3424) and `collectOwCallsStmt` likewise (src/codegen.c:3556), but `countOwSites` has no `ST_DOMAIN` case and falls into `default: return 0`, so it answers 0 for a body whose only `@overwrite` is inside a domain block. The two consumers then disagree: `f->owSites` (this count) gates `needOw` in codegen (src/codegen.c:7188-7192), which is the only thing that emits `typedef struct extc_owcell {...}` (src/codegen.c:7389), while codegen's own `owNow = collectOwSites(f->body)` (src/codegen.c:4730-4731, sized by the same divergent walker) does contain the site and emits `extc_owcell __extc_ow0 = ...` for it (src/codegen.c:4846-4852). Result: generated C that names an undeclared type; `./build/extc f.extc -o out.c` still exits 0, so the user only finds out when the C compiler runs. (`owLocal` is set to true for every function this pass sees, which is why the stale `f->owSites` count does not also corrupt the `__extc_owarg%d` parameter list here; the typedef is enough to break the product.)
findings.trigger: Any function whose only `@overwrite` binding sits inside a `d.run { ... }` domain block, e.g. `main` with `d.run { @overwrite var buf = new [8]u8  buf[0] = u8(1) }`.

findings.title: Trait/impl conformance compares return types only when BOTH are non-void, so a trait method returning a value may be implemented as `void` (and vice versa): generated C does not compile
findings.why: A NULL return type is extC's representation of `void` (`resolveSignature`: `if (f->ret && ttIs(f->ret, "void")) f->ret = NULL;`). The guard `if (wantR && haveR && ...)` therefore compares only two non-void types and silently accepts `void` against any type, even though the very next lines assert that the return type "is part of the contract and must match exactly". The dynamic-dispatch table is built from the trait's signature (the emitted vtable is `int64_t (*enc)(void *)`), so the implementation is wrapped in a thunk that must produce a value from a `void` call -> invalid C. This is not a corner of the language: `trait Codec { fn enc(self: ref Self) -> i64 }` + `impl Codec for box { fn enc(self: ref box) { ... } }` is exactly the author error the check exists to name.
findings.trigger: A trait method with a receiver and a non-void return type, and an `impl ... for <struct>` whose method has the same name/arity but no return type (or the reverse: trait `-> void`, impl returning a value). Requires the trait to be dispatched (e.g. `dyn Trait(v).method()`), which is what makes the thunk be generated.

findings.title: Trait/impl conformance is skipped entirely for targets without a StructDef (builtins and views): `impl Trait for i64` / `for slice<u8>` may contradict the trait
findings.why: `structOf` returns non-NULL only for `TY_STRUCT`/`TY_GENERIC` (src/check_lookup.c:418-422); for `TY_BUILTIN` (i64, ...) and for view/builtin-generic targets such as `slice<u8>` it returns NULL, so the whole `impl Trait for T` signature comparison is skipped for them. The dispatch table is generated from the TRAIT's signature and the impl is reached through a thunk that converts arguments/returns to the trait's types, so a mismatched impl is silently coerced instead of rejected: `trait Codec { fn enc(self: ref Self) -> i64 }` + `impl Codec for i64 { fn enc(self: ref i64) -> bool { return *self > i64(0) } }` is accepted and `dyn Codec(i64(5)).enc()` prints `1`; with `-> void` on `slice<u8>` the generated C does not compile at all (`extc_th$Codec$slice_u8$enc`: void value not ignored). The trait's declared contract is the only signature a caller can see, so accepting an implementation that contradicts it is the same class of hole the check exists to close.
findings.trigger: Any `impl Trait for <builtin|view>`: `impl Codec for i64 { ... }`, `impl Codec for slice<u8> { ... }` (the last one is exercised by the repo's own tests/instimpl/t_trait.extc). Mismatched parameter types (position >= 2 or a receiver-less method) and mismatched return types are both accepted.

findings.title: `funcReachesItself` has no memo and explores every call path up to depth 64: exponential compile time for an `@inline` function over a fan-out call graph
findings.why: The walk returns as soon as it literally reaches `f`, so when `f` is NOT recursive every path of the callee DAG is enumerated: there is no visited set and no memo, and the only bound is the depth cap of 64. With a call graph of L levels where each function calls two distinct functions of the next level, the number of visited paths is 2^L. The function is called once per `@inline` function (src/check_top.c:5879), and its result is only a yes/no answer that memoization over (function) would give in linear time. Measured on the compiler's own binary: L=24 -> 0.10 s, L=30 -> 2.2 s, L=32 -> 8.8 s, L=34 -> 36.3 s, L=36 -> still running after 60 s (about 4x per +2 levels); the cap of 64 puts the worst case around 2^64 steps.
findings.trigger: One `@inline` function on top of a DAG with fan-out (each function calling two distinct functions of the next level); no recursion is needed, and the callees are deduplicated by pointer, so the two callees of a level must be distinct functions. 68 small functions are enough for a 36-second compile of an otherwise trivial module.
findings.repro:
python3 - <<'EOF'
N=36; src=""
for i in range(1,N+1):
    for tag in ("l","r"):
        pre="@inline " if (i==1 and tag=="l") else ""
        body=f"  l{i+1}()\n  r{i+1}()\n" if i<N else "  return\n"
        src+=f"{pre}fn {tag}{i}() {{\n{body}}}\n\n"
src+="fn main() { l1()  r1() }\n"
open("/tmp/x/dd36.extc","w").write(src)
EOF
time timeout 60 ./build/extc /tmp/x/dd36.extc -o /tmp/x/dd36.c   # does not finish (same file with N=34 takes 36.3 s, N=24 0.10 s)

findings.title: Trait/impl parameter comparison starts at index 1 unconditionally: for a receiver-less method the first real parameter is never compared
findings.why: `j = 1` skips the receiver, which is right only when the method HAS a receiver. The code above has just accepted two shapes (`funcIsMethod(want) == funcIsMethod(have)`, equal arity), and a trait method may legitimately be declared without `self` (`fn zero() -> i64`, used by tests/errors/dyn_assoc_dispatch.extc); for such a method parameter 0 is an ordinary parameter and is never compared, so the "parameter types are part of the contract and must match exactly" diagnostic cannot fire for it. The first version of this check would have been written as `for (j = funcIsMethod(want) ? 1 : 0; ...)`.
findings.trigger: A trait method without a receiver that takes at least one parameter, implemented with a different type at that position: `trait Conv { fn conv(x: i64) -> i64 }` + `impl Conv for box { fn conv(x: bool) -> i64 { ... } }`. The program is accepted with no diagnostic (the call would have to be written `box::conv(...)`, which is then type-checked against the impl, so no wrong code was observed, but the conformance error the check exists to report is never produced).

coverage_notes: Read all of src/check_top.c lines 1-1720 line by line (the file is actually 6885 lines, so this is the first chunk), plus the callers/callees elsewhere that the range depends on. Verified as correct (or at least not demonstrably wrong) after cross-checking other files: funcTParams/resolveSignature (ctx switch and void-to-NULL normalisation match ttResolve's contract); checkDeclarations' duplicate rules (struct/field/method/type/variant and the operator right-operand exemption, including the `params.len >= 2` guard); checkMethodShape (self-type test for struct vs builtin holder, isAssoc inference, first-parameter rule); the whole @overwrite/where-does-the-arena-go machinery in the range (stmtHasNew/exprHasNew, needsHomeInExpr, cnameInExpr, bodyReaches, closeReach/roundOverModule, computeEffectsTransitive's cycle and completeness discipline, markCallHomeIfEscaping/setCallArenaArg/setCallZoneArg/callHomeDepth) -- I confirmed that every resolved call kind (EX_CALL/EX_METHOD/EX_ASSOC) goes through setCallArenaArg in check_expr.c, so arenaArg is never left at its zero default, and that the `homeDepth == 0` (no mut-ref destination) case is settled by the pending-site pass; valueMayCarryRef/stmtStoresThroughDeref (conservative directions checked); exprMakesPool/stmtMakesPool/calleeMakesPool/calleeCreatesPool (walked against the AST kind list and against codegen's zone-hook site, including the ST_DOMAIN/descendBlocks pair); exprIsFresh/exprIsPoolBlock/vecHasName; collectLoopSites (all Stmt kinds covered). Not proven, listed for the record: (a) computeEffectsTransitive merges a callee's parameter-indexed masks into the caller's by bit position (lines 1162-1167) with no call-site argument mapping, which looks wrong when the argument positions differ (`wrap(a,b){ inner(b) }` gives wrap bit 0 instead of bit 1); I could not build a repro because the refDepth checks caught every shape I tried, so I did not report it. (b) `checkCallRefArgs`'s fallback `h = (homeDepth > 0) ? homeDepth : c->scopes.len` (line 1273) is maximally permissive when a callee has homeAddr/homeCont bits but no measurable `mut ref` destination; again every shape I built was caught by the separate refDepth/escape pass. (c) checkDeclarations is O(n^2) over structs/functions/types (measured: 8000 functions -> 0.155 s total, curve consistent with quadratic but with a small constant) -- not worth a finding. The two findings at lines 6019-6026 and 6326-6334 are just past the nominal 1-1720 boundary of my chunk; they consume exactly the `argDepth` records that `callHomeDepth` (line 1606, in range) produces, they are duplicated in the two passes that share the pattern, and the first one has an ASan-verified repro, so I reported them rather than drop a P0.
